question: Move the AED at P.S. 184M Shuang Wen into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 184M Shuang Wen (School, ZIP 10002) has a registered AED at "Front Entrance".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.21 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 5 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 5 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 4, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 163 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly addresses a documented gap. The school's current hours mean it's unreachable during 113 of 168 weekly hours when students aren't present [E3]. Last year, an expected 1.21 cardiac arrests occurred in the surrounding area when every nearby AED was closed [E4]—ranking this location fifth among NYC schools for this problem. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. The five other AEDs nearby offer no 24/7 alternative [E5]. A street-wall cabinet would serve the community around the clock, filling a real access gap that current resources don't.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The data does show a real gap—1.21 expected cardiac arrests yearly occur when nearby AEDs are closed [E4]—but moving this particular AED may not be the best fix. The fire station 163 meters away [E8] is already staffed 24/7 and could potentially host an AED without removing one from the school building where it's currently registered and accessible during high-occupancy hours [E1]. We don't know the cabinet's cost, vandalism risk, or whether after-hours school access is already possible [E9]. Before committing resources here, we should explore whether FDNY Station 4 can serve this gap more reliably than an outdoor cabinet.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The fire station alternative deserves exploration, but it doesn't eliminate the need to act here. Station 4 is 163 meters away [E8]—outside the two-minute walking radius where most bystanders can reach an AED in time. The skeptic's proposal also assumes a new AED would be placed there, not that an existing one would be moved. Meanwhile, this school's current AED remains inaccessible 113 of 168 weekly hours [E3], and last year an expected 1.21 cardiac arrests happened when all nearby devices were closed [E4]. A 24/7 cabinet on the school's street wall keeps the existing resource available during school hours while filling the documented after-hours gap. These aren't mutually exclusive solutions.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate is right that 163 meters exceeds a typical two-minute walk and that solutions needn't be mutually exclusive. But the core question remains whether moving this AED is the right choice. The 1.21 expected annual arrests [E4] represents the gap, yet we don't know where those calls actually occurred within the ZIP code [E9]—they may cluster elsewhere, making this school wall a suboptimal location. A fire station AED wouldn't replace this one; it would add capacity. Before relocating an AED already registered and accessible during peak school hours [E1], we should cost the cabinet, assess vandalism risk [E9], and confirm whether Station 4 placement is feasible. That might solve the problem without removing coverage from where students gather.

verdict.summary: Documented gap exists (1.21 expected arrests yearly when nearby AEDs closed), but moving this AED requires cost, vandalism, and location data before deciding between relocation versus complementary placement at nearby fire station.
verdict.strongestFor: School AED unreachable 113/168 weekly hours [E3]; 1.21 expected cardiac arrests occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; 66.5% survival with public AED versus 43.0% without [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual 2025 call locations unknown within ZIP [E9]; fire station 163 m away [E8] could add capacity without removing school access [E1]; cabinet cost and vandalism risk undetermined [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Obtain: (1) exact 2025 cardiac-arrest call locations within ZIP; (2) cabinet cost and vandalism data; (3) FDNY Station 4 feasibility for 24/7 AED placement.
